job: Power steering fluid service (drain and refill or exchange)
held_reason: Held at review after two attempts: the spot check confirmed the quantities (Subaru 0.7 US qt, GM 3 qt of DEXRON-VI for the Traverse) but could not confirm which fluid the 2009 Impreza and 2010 Forester manuals specify for power steering (the 'Recommended fluid' note sits on a page headed 'Brake fluid' and the page before it would not load), so two classes price a fluid that is not confirmed for them. To finish: load the manual page that names the power steering fluid under its own heading, or switch the two classes to examples whose maker document states both quantity and fluid.
unit: per vehicle with hydraulic power steering: replacing the power steering fluid by draining and refilling through the reservoir or return hose, or by a simple exchange, then bleeding the air out. Parts are the fluid only, costed at the quantity the vehicle's maker prints: one fill of the system as listed in the owner's manual (0.7 US quart on the Subaru examples, 0.9 US quart on the Volvo, bought as one whole bottle) or the amount the maker's bulletin says a flush may take (3 quarts on the GM example). Not included: cleaning chemicals or additives, a pump, hoses, rack or gear, belt, leak diagnosis or leak repair. Cars with electric power steering have no power steering fluid and do not need this service

economy.example: 2009 Subaru Impreza (hydraulic power steering, 0.7 US quart system capacity, one quart bottle of Subaru ATF-HP/PS fluid)

parts_src.what: Quantity, maker document for this vehicle: the 2009 Subaru Impreza owner's manual, Capacities page (page 375 of the manual as shown on a manual-hosting site, not Subaru's own site), lists 'Power steering fluid' '0.7 US qt (0.7 liter, 0.6 Imp qt)'. This is the capacity of the system, one fill; a flush that runs fluid through until it comes out clean uses more

Cross-check: fluid type. The 2009 Impreza owner's manual page that follows the power steering fluid section (page 342 on the same manual-hosting site) carries a 'Recommended fluid' note reading 'Use one of the following types of automatic transmission fluid': 'SUBARU ATF Type-HP' or 'Dexron III Type Automatic Transmission Fluid'. In the page text loaded this note sits above the brake fluid heading and is not labelled with its section, so it is taken, not proven, to be the power steering fluid note

LOW and HIGH: Genuine Subaru ATF-HP/PS Fluid SOA427V1500 (a 1-quart bottle, size confirmed on the retailer page below), MSRP $9.38 (HIGH), discounted $7.71 (LOW). One bottle covers the 0.7 US quart capacity, so 1 x the bottle price. The low is the genuine fluid at a discount, not an aftermarket fluid: no aftermarket fluid page naming this vehicle was loaded. The page prints no vehicle fitment list; the part's own name marks it as the power steering (PS) fluid

Cross-check: retailer, 'Subaru (OEM) Automatic Transmission & Power Steering Fluid (1 Quart)' SOA427V1500 at $9.38, 'recommended for use in 4-EAT and 5-EAT Subaru Automatic Transmissions and Subaru Power Steering Systems'; fitment listed as 'Universal'. Matches the high end

finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures. This service applies only to vehicles with hydraulic power steering; most newer cars have electric power steering and no fluid, which is why the examples are older. Shops usually sell it at a set menu price, not as parts plus clocked labor. Built totals (fluid + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2009 Subaru Impreza and midsize 2010 Subaru Forester about $68-$169 each (one quart bottle of Subaru ATF-HP/PS fluid at $7.71-$9.38, 0.5-1.0 hr); truck class 2012 Chevrolet Traverse about $150-$209 (3 quarts of DEXRON-VI at $13.99-$16.22, 0.9-1.0 hr); luxury 2009 Volvo S60 about $87-$201 (one 1-liter bottle of Volvo fluid at $26.98-$41.06, 0.5-1.0 hr). A fair plain-language range is roughly $70-$210. Against the benchmarks: FIXD ($95-$125) sits inside the range, and YourMechanic ($168-$212) and Sunbit ($170-$205) sit at the upper end; all three fall inside or touch the built range. The six posted menu prices ($69.99-$207.88) span almost exactly the same range. How solid the figures are, stated plainly. Fluid quantity now comes from a maker document for every example: the Subaru and Volvo owner's manuals print the power steering system capacity (0.7 and 0.9 US quart), and a GM bulletin that names the 2009-2012 Traverse says a flush may take 3 quarts. Two cautions: the Subaru and Volvo manuals were read on a manual-hosting site, not the makers' own sites, and the GM quantity was read on the first research pass and could not be reloaded on the second. The Subaru and Volvo figures are one fill of the system; a shop that flushes fluid through until it runs clean uses more (the do-it-yourself guide cited says a proper flush takes about twice what the system holds), and one extra bottle would add $7.71-$9.38 on the Subaru and $26.98-$41.06 on the Volvo. Labor: the truck-class low end is the one manufacturer time found, GM's 0.9 hr 'Flush and Bleed Power Steering System', printed in a bulletin that covers the 2012-2013 Traverse by name; it is a warranty time for a cold-weather noise repair. No Subaru or Volvo time for this job was found, so the three car classes rest on one technician's statement in a February 2000 trade article that a Honda flush takes him about half an hour (low) and one regional chain's statement that a flush can take up to 1 hour (high); neither is a flat-rate book time or for the example vehicle, and a do-it-yourself guide says 1 to 2 hours. Prices: every low end is the genuine fluid at a discounted price, not an aftermarket fluid, because no aftermarket fluid page naming these vehicles was loaded; the Subaru fluid page prints no fitment list, the Volvo fluid is matched through the part number the owner's manual names, and the GM fluid is matched by the DEXRON-VI name in the bulletin. The truck class uses a large crossover SUV because no maker document printing a fluid quantity for a pickup was found (GM's Silverado bulletin gives the 0.9 hr time but no quantity). An estimate is not a quote. Posted menu prices loaded on 2026-11-20 from six sellers' own pages (three dealers, one regional chain and two local multi-shop independents in Michigan, West Virginia, New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, North Carolina and Georgia) run from $69.99 to $207.88 for the whole car, mostly before tax and shop fees: $69.99-$99.99 at the Michigan independent, $79.95 and $99.00 at two dealers, $99.99 at the chain (a chemical-cleaner flush, marked as a different service), $158.99 at the North Carolina independent and $207.88 at a Honda dealer; national chains were not searched because they do not print this price.
extras: A quote often adds shop supplies, fluid disposal and sales tax. Many shops sell a machine exchange with a cleaning chemical or a conditioner additive instead of a plain drain and refill, which costs more. If the visit is for a whine, stiff steering or a leak, expect a separate diagnosis fee, and a leaking hose, pump, rack or steering gear or a worn belt is quoted separately. Some vehicles need a specific fluid (Honda and Acura fluid, a synthetic fluid such as Pentosin on many European cars and cold-climate GM trucks, or automatic transmission fluid on others), and the wrong one can damage seals. Vehicles with electric power steering do not need this service at all.
